findings.antecedent: Animal spatial circumstances (disrupting personal/social spatial domains)
findings.quote: The experiments influenced by these ideas sought evidence of psychological stress or aggression as automatic responses to very close individual distances, territorial invasions, or overcrowded conditions.

findings.antecedent: Unusual spatial circumstances (humans, e.g., close individual distances, territorial invasions, overcrowded conditions)
findings.quote: Several studies in fact found a relationship between spatial circumstances and heightened arousal as measured by self-reports and machines (Aiello et al 1975; Baxter & Deanovitch 1970; McBride et al 1965; Smith & Haythorn 1972; Evans 1978).
There is no consistent evidence, however, that abnormal spatial situations elicit specific kinds of responses among humans.

findings.consequent: Interpersonal distances, preferred densities, touching behavior
findings.quote: Hall (1966:13, 172–73) divided the peoples of the world into two groups, based on similar statements that Hediger (see Hall 1966) made about the animal kingdom. 'Contact cultures' are consid-ered to be highly involved in their interactions and thus use small interac-tion distances, like high densities, and engage in frequent touching (Arabs and Latins were used as examples). 'Noncontact cultures,' on the other hand, shun touching, dislike high densities, and avoid close interpersonal distances (Northern Europeans and North Americans were placed in this category).

The teachers in these settings, who rewarded what they saw as proper interpersonal distance, punished children who approached others too closely, and physi-cally prompted individuals who maintained distances too far from others (see also Bailey et al 1973). The teachers in these two settings shared similar values and thus provided similar learning experiences in regard to spatial behavior.

findings.antecedent: Physical characteristics of a setting (buildings, design)
findings.quote: this view assumes that the physical characteristics of a setting per se have a large influence on our attitudes and actions, rather than our environments 'triggering' a biological or cultural trait.

findings.antecedent: Design factors (e.g., public spaces perceived as residents' domain, fostering territoriality)
findings.consequent: Reduced crime, community monitoring, healthy/happy tenants
findings.quote: The belief was that 'good' design can lead to healthy and happy tenants, while 'bad' design can have disastrous effects on residents.

findings.antecedent: Design (low-rise, high-density, shared facilities, forced contact)
findings.consequent: Social interaction, community spirit, cooperation, communality
findings.quote: Similar research indicates that design can force spatial proximity, and this inevitably leads to social interaction and community spirit.

findings.consequent: Social and psychological difficulties (rather than density per se)
findings.quote: There has also been a view expressed that it is environmental design that causes social and psychological difficulties and not density per se (Mitchell 1974).
Osmond (1957, 1959) coined the terms 'sociopetal' and 'sociofu-gal' to suggest that interior design can encourage or discourage group formation.

findings.antecedent: Perceived situation (room design, imagined ongoing activity)
findings.quote: Not only did individu-als vary the densities with room designs but, importantly, also with the imagined ongoing activity.
Stokols et al (1977) found that perceived crowding was related to poorer academic performance and health among university students.

only a moderate amount of the vari-ance seems to be explained by objective household space (i.e. persons per room), which indicates that objective density is only part of the spatial problem in these homes.
perceived household crowding has an independent effect on measures of housing satisfaction (i.e. when account-ing for persons per room), including an impact on preferred mobility

findings.consequent: Increased room density (without adverse psychological effects), decreased visible social stimuli
findings.quote: she found that subjects placed more figures within a space as the number of partitions increased. This indicated to her that room density may be increased (with no adverse psychological effects) when the number of visible social stimuli decrease.

findings.consequent: Faster pedestrian walking speed (attempt to minimize social stimulation)
findings.quote: A study conducted by Bornstein & Bornstein (1976) found that pedestrians walked through the streets faster as city size increased, which suggested to the authors that the more crowded individuals were trying to minimize the level of social stimulation they experienced
Yet another field experiment in a department store in New York City suggested that people had task and performance deficits due to overstimulation in dense shopping environments

findings.consequent: Involvement in primary relationships (friends, family, organizations)
findings.quote: individuals experiencing residential crowding do not withdraw from primary relationships (friends, social networks, family, organizations), though they seem to decrease involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature (reactions to strangers, neighboring, meeting new people), which indicates a cost-effective method of limiting social overload

findings.consequent: Involvement in secondary social encounters (strangers, neighboring, meeting new people)
findings.quote: individuals experiencing residential crowding do not withdraw from primary relationships (friends, social networks, family, organizations), though they seem to decrease involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature (reactions to strangers, neighboring, meeting new people), which indicates a cost-effective method of limiting social overload

findings.antecedent: Lack of predictability and controllability (environmental stressor like noise)
findings.consequent: Stress response, aftereffects (e.g., decreased cognitive abilities)
findings.quote: it was the lack of predictability and controllability of the experience that caused a stress response, and experimental manipulations of these variables pro-vided strong evidence for these conclusions.

findings.antecedent: Perceived control (over a stressor, even without actual control)
findings.quote: the mere percep-tion of control over the noise stimulus (without actual control during the situation) exerted a significant influence over behavioral responses to the situation.
Crowding has recently been viewed as a situation in which individuals are confronted with environmental circumstances beyond their control.

findings.antecedent: Manipulated perceived control (e.g., ability to leave a crowded room)
findings.consequent: Aftereffects of stress exposure (e.g., poor task performance)
findings.quote: Sher-rod (1974) manipulated perceived control in a crowding experiment (i.e. ability to leave the room), and found that the aftereffects of stress exposure (i.e. poor task performance) were present in the group that lacked a sense of control over the crowded situation.
A field study found that chronic household crowding created task deficits among children (Rodin 1976).

findings.antecedent: Amount of control individuals are given during group tasks
findings.quote: Other studies indicated that perceptions of crowding were also affected by the amount of control individuals were given during group tasks (Rodin et al 1976).
Therefore, if people's perceptions of control are increased, the negative aspects of spatial shortages can be alleviated

findings.antecedent: Low social status/power (e.g., urban poor, children)
findings.consequent: Claim to space (when in high demand)
findings.quote: people of low status (e.g. the urban poor, the child in the crowded household) may have less of a claim to space when it is in high demand than do people of high status
Actual power over spatial use should minimize overload and allow one to conduct desired activities with less interference

findings.antecedent: Space shortage in a stable, status-differentiated group (e.g., family)
findings.consequent: Greater control over space use and activities (e.g., scheduling, regulating utilization)
findings.quote: A common response of a stable, status-differentiated group experi-encing a shortage of space is greater control over space use and activities in its territory.

findings.antecedent: Social meanings attached to environments (through interactions, socialization)
findings.quote: The social meanings that people attach to environments through their interactions and ongoing socialization thus would play an important role in determining human spatial responses

findings.antecedent: People's imagery of spaces (fantasy vs. reality)
findings.consequent: Coping with existing circumstances, imagining better positions
findings.quote: Sometimes the images people have of their spaces are more fantasy than reality, and Lym (1978a,b) argues that people develop these images in order to cope with the existing circumstances and imagine themselves in better positions.

findings.consequent: Spatial differentiation, mechanisms for controlling movement across boundaries (privacy)
findings.quote: role differentiation demands some degree of spatial differentiation within territories (Lym 1978b) and a mechanism for controlling movement across boundaries.

findings.antecedent: Disagreement on space allocation (for role enactments)
findings.consequent: Interpersonal tension, role interference, psychological stress
findings.quote: Varying images of territorial allotments can produce both interpersonal tension and role interference.

findings.antecedent: Short supply of household space (lack of room or privacy)
findings.consequent: Role conflict, incomplete role performances, intrusions, blocking desired role enactments, loss of control over boundary mechanisms
findings.quote: If there is not enough room or privacy to conduct desired roles alone and with others, competition for space use may occur. Undoubtedly, the possibilities of incomplete role performances, intrusions, and the blocking of desired role enactments are heightened.
